summary:
Outright International records same-sex relations as legal throughout Italy for men and women. The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, and Italy has had an equal age of consent for homosexual and heterosexual acts since before the 20th century.

Italy's position on sexual orientation and gender identity rests on court rulings and sectoral statutes rather than a single comprehensive law. No Italian law explicitly bans transphobic discrimination, and ILGA-Europe's 2021 report noted the absence of nationwide protection covering goods and services, leaving transgender people exposed to discrimination in housing, education and health care. Sexual-orientation discrimination in employment has been illegal nationwide since July 2003 under Legislative Decree no. 216 of 2003, implementing EU Directive 2000/78/EC; the exemptions for police, armed forces and rescue services were removed by Law no. 101 of 2008. A Rome court ruled on 15 January 2023 that firing a trans professor amounted to sex discrimination.

ILGA-Europe's 2026 Annual Review documents that homophobic and transphobic violence continued during 2025, including organised dating-app entrapment schemes in which groups lure victims and then assault or rob them. Progetto Gionata characterises transphobia as the most severe and most widespread discrimination confronting transgender people in Italy, which is consistent with the pattern recorded by monitors rather than with isolated incidents.

The most serious traveller-specific finding is the sexual assault of young transgender tourists in Campania. ANSA reports that the convictions for the assault were upheld on appeal in April 2026, a court outcome that affirms accountability for violence against trans visitors rather than impunity for it.

Violence by state agents has also been prosecuted. In July 2024 a Milan traffic officer was sentenced to 10 months for beating a transgender woman with a baton.

Official hostility shapes the environment around that violence. The Education Ministry omitted LGBTI persecution from its Holocaust Remembrance Day circulars for a second year, and a cardinal publicly described homosexual acts as a mortal sin. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 records political rhetoric hostile to LGBT people as contributing to a hostile environment in Italy.

The courts have moved in the opposite direction on several points. In March 2025 the Civil Court of Asti recognised, for the first time, physical and psychological harm resulting from homophobic mistreatment.

Legal gender recognition has been available since 1982, when Italy became the sixth country worldwide to allow it, and since 21 May 2015 neither sterilisation nor sex reassignment surgery has been required. On 23 July 2024 the Constitutional Court, in judgment no. 143, first recognised non-binary individuals as rights-holders under Articles 2, 3 and 32 but declined to add a non-binary registry marker, holding that only Parliament can alter the male/female binary; the same judgment struck down the requirement of judicial authorisation for gender-affirming surgery after a legal sex change. On 14 April 2025 the Supreme Court of Cassation ordered Italian identity cards to use the gender-neutral term "genitori" rather than "mother" and "father" for children with same-sex parents, finding the previous wording discriminatory.

Cross-dressing is legal. The fascist penal code of the 1920s–1940s banned it and police targeted trans people, and in 2006 a police officer was reportedly dismissed for cross-dressing in public while off duty.

Italy recognises persecution based on sexual orientation or gender identity as grounds for asylum under the 1951 Geneva Convention and the EU Qualification Directive 2011/95/EU, and Decree-Law No. 130/2020, in force 22 October 2020, simplified asylum procedures and reinforced protection for vulnerable groups including those persecuted on those grounds.
tangentialFactors:
Regional statutes have filled part of the gap left by the absence of a nationwide law, with nine regions legislating anti-discrimination protection between 2004 and 2024: Tuscany, Liguria, Marche, Sicily, Piedmont, Umbria, Emilia-Romagna, Campania and Apulia. Protection therefore varies by where a visitor is, and the most recent regional statute dates to 2024.

Legislative attempts to broaden protection have repeatedly failed. A bill banning homophobic and transphobic advertising in streets and on vehicles passed the Chamber of Deputies 271–16 on 28 October 2021 and the Senate 190–34 on 4 November, was signed by President Mattarella and took effect 10 November 2021; the government forced a single up-or-down vote on the whole bill, so MPs who opposed that provision had to vote for it. A broader anti-discrimination and hate-crime bill passed the Chamber 265–193 on 4 November 2020 but died in the Senate on 27 October 2021 by a 131–154 secret ballot.

Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 also records constraints on the rule of law and on civil society in Italy, which bear on how reliably protections are enforced in practice.

Attitudinal and institutional signals run in both directions. Pew found in 2013 that 86% of Italians aged 18–29 accepted homosexuality, against 67% of those over 50. In May 2026 AGESCI, Italy's largest Catholic scout association, decided that sexual orientation and gender identity can no longer exclude adults from leadership and educational roles, after three years of internal debate.
localsOnly:
The Ludwig Boltzmann Institute published a national report in July 2025 on LGBTIQ detainees in Italy, covering homolesbobitransphobia and discrimination, pathways to gender affirmation, same-sex relationships, and the legal and policy framework governing LGBTIQ people in Italian detention.

A 2026 thematic analysis in Frontiers in Psychiatry examined transgender identity and psychiatric care in Italian prisons, identifying systemic gaps and institutional challenges for incarcerated trans people. Both sources address people in state custody rather than short-term visitors.

Health care coverage is established for residents: since February 2019 puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones have been provided free of charge under the National Health Service, and since 2020 hormone therapy has been fully covered. In 2018 the Italian National Bioethics Committee and the Italian Medicines Agency backed puberty blockers for adolescents with gender dysphoria case by case with safeguards; access requires medical evaluation, parental consent and exhaustion of other interventions, a position supported by the Italian Society of Endocrinology, the Italian Academy of Pediatrics and six other paediatric and adolescent medical societies. Gay and bisexual men have been allowed to donate blood since 2001.

Courts have extended gender recognition in specific circumstances. Courts in Trento (15 February 2023) permitted legal gender change for transgender minors with parental consent and psychological consultation, and Trapani (6 July 2023) allowed a name and gender change with no surgery or hormones.

Same-sex marriages performed abroad are registered as civil unions rather than marriages, per a Court of Cassation decision of May 2018. Citing the Constitutional Court's 2010 ruling that recognised same-sex couples as a "legitimate social formation," the Court of Cassation ordered a questura to grant a residence permit to an Algerian citizen married to a same-sex Spanish spouse.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses entry, visa or border-screening procedures, and none describes whether gender markers on foreign passports are checked or questioned at Italian points of entry. That layer of the visitor risk assessment remains unsourced rather than assessed as low-risk.

The practical reach of the 2021 advertising ban and of the regional anti-discrimination statutes in enforcement is not sourced here; the inventory records their passage and scope, not how often they are applied.

Whether the detention findings from the Ludwig Boltzmann report and the Frontiers in Psychiatry analysis extend to short-term visitors held in custody is not stated by either source and is unresolved.

Access to Italian health services for a non-resident trans visitor, including continuity of hormone therapy, is not covered by the sources, which describe the National Health Service scheme without addressing eligibility for visitors.

The Intrepid Travel page presents Italy as an LGBTQIA+ destination for its travellers but carries no safety finding specific to Italy, and so supports no assessment either way.
